items.prompt: What's the key difference between line coverage and mutation score?
choices: Coverage measures whether a line executed; mutation score measures whether a test would actually fail if that line's logic were subtly wrong
Coverage measures how fast tests run; mutation score measures memory usage
They measure exactly the same thing, just expressed with different units
Mutation score is just coverage recalculated per file instead of per line
items.explanation: Coverage is about execution (did this line run at all); mutation score is about verification (would a test notice if this line's logic were wrong). A line can be fully covered and still never actually checked.
items.reference:
▶️ Coverage — did this line run?
🧬 Mutation score — would a test fail if this line were subtly wrong?

Why: a suite can run every line without checking the value any of them produced — that's the exact gap mutation testing is built to expose.

items.prompt: A file has 100% line coverage. What does that alone guarantee about test quality?
choices: Nothing about whether the tests would catch a subtle logic bug — only that every line executed at least once
That every possible bug in the file would be caught by the suite
That the file's mutation score is also 100%
That every test contains at least one assertion
items.explanation: 100% coverage is fully compatible with a suite that never asserts on the values that matter — coverage is silent on assertion quality entirely.
items.reference:
▶️ Coverage — did this line run?
🧬 Mutation score — would a test fail if this line were subtly wrong?

Why: a suite can run every line without checking the value any of them produced — that's the exact gap mutation testing is built to expose.

items.prompt: Per L1's Scenario, the shipping-fee calculator had 95% coverage and a boundary bug shipped anyway. What best explains this?
choices: Coverage counted the buggy line as "tested" because it ran, but no test actually checked the value it produced
Coverage tools are generally unreliable for JavaScript
The bug was in a line that had 0% coverage
The team had disabled their tests before shipping
items.explanation: The buggy line executed during the test run, so coverage counted it as tested — but no assertion actually checked the value at the exact boundary where the bug lived.
items.reference:
▶️ Coverage — did this line run?
🧬 Mutation score — would a test fail if this line were subtly wrong?

Why: a suite can run every line without checking the value any of them produced — that's the exact gap mutation testing is built to expose.

items.prompt: What is a "mutant" in mutation testing?
choices: A copy of the code with one small, deliberate change applied, like flipping one comparison operator
A test that fails randomly for no clear reason
A developer's very first commit to a new project
A function that currently has zero tests written for it
items.explanation: A mutant is a deliberately, mechanically modified version of the code — one small change at one location — used to probe whether the test suite would notice.

items.prompt: Where does a mutation-testing tool get the list of possible mutants to generate?
choices: From a catalog of mutation operators — fixed rules like "replace `>` with `>=`" modeled on common real mistakes
It generates them completely at random with no fixed rules at all
A developer manually writes out every single mutant by hand
It copies mutants from a public database of past production incidents
items.explanation: Tools apply a fixed catalog of mutation operators mechanically across the code — the operators are modeled on real, common programmer mistakes, not random corruption.

items.prompt: What does it mean when a mutant is "killed"?
choices: At least one test in the suite fails when run against the mutated code
The mutant causes the program to crash on startup
The mutant is deleted from the tool's mutant list before it can run
Every test in the suite still passes against the mutant
items.explanation: "Killed" specifically means a test caught the mutation — at least one test failed that would have passed against the correct, unmutated code.

items.prompt: If a mutant is killed, what has actually been demonstrated?
choices: The test suite would catch that specific kind of bug if it were introduced into the real code
The original code definitely has no bugs anywhere in the file
The mutant itself was generated incorrectly by the tool
Line coverage for that spot has increased
items.explanation: A kill only proves the suite catches that one specific mutation — it's evidence about test quality at that spot, not a global correctness proof for the whole file.

items.prompt: What does it mean when a mutant "survives"?
choices: Every test in the suite still passes against the mutated code — the suite has a real gap at that exact spot
The mutant was too small for any tool to detect
The original code definitely contains a bug
The test suite ran out of time before finishing
items.explanation: A surviving mutant means no test in the suite distinguishes the mutated behavior from the correct behavior at that spot — a concrete gap in what's actually being verified.

items.prompt: A mutant survives at a specific line. What's the most useful next step?
choices: Treat it as a pointer to a concrete test gap and consider writing a test that would distinguish correct from mutated behavior there
Delete that line of code, since a survivor proves it's unnecessary
Ignore it — a single surviving mutant never matters
Immediately assume production is broken and roll back the last deploy
items.explanation: A survivor is diagnostic, not an emergency — it names an exact spot and kind of bug the current suite can't see, useful as a direct pointer to where a new test should go.

items.prompt: How is mutation score calculated?
choices: Killed mutants divided by total non-equivalent mutants, as a percentage
Total mutants divided by lines of code in the file
Number of tests divided by number of mutants generated
Coverage percentage multiplied by the number of tests
items.explanation: Mutation score is killed / total non-equivalent mutants — equivalent mutants (which can never be killed by any test) are excluded from the denominator.

items.prompt: A file generates 40 mutants; 30 are killed, 10 survive, and none are equivalent. What's the mutation score?
items.explanation: 30 killed ÷ 40 total non-equivalent mutants = 75%.

items.prompt: In L1's Scenario, the existing test "ran" the buggy line. Why didn't that count as catching the bug?
choices: Running a line and checking the value it produces are different things — the test never inspected the output at the point the bug lived
The test framework itself had a bug
The line technically never executed during the test run
The test suite was disabled in CI at the time
items.explanation: The line ran (satisfying coverage), but no assertion checked the value it produced at the exact boundary where the bug lived — execution and verification are different things.

items.prompt: What's the general lesson L1's Scenario is meant to teach?
choices: A high coverage percentage is a weak signal for test quality — mutation score is a much stronger one, because it directly measures whether tests would catch a real bug
Coverage tools should never be used for anything
Every codebase needs a 100% mutation score before it can ship
Mutation testing replaces the need to write tests at all
items.explanation: The point isn't that coverage is worthless — it's that coverage alone is a weak proxy for test quality, and mutation score measures the thing coverage can't: whether tests would actually catch a bug.

items.prompt: Per L2's flowchart, what happens immediately after a mutant is generated?
choices: The full test suite is run against that mutant
The mutant is immediately deleted without being tested
Coverage is recalculated for the whole file
The original code is permanently replaced by the mutant
items.explanation: Each mutant is a separate hypothesis tested by rerunning the full suite against that one mutated version of the code.

items.prompt: Per L2's flowchart, what determines whether a mutant is recorded as killed or survived?
choices: Whether any test in the suite fails when run against that specific mutant
Whether the mutant compiles without errors
How many lines the mutant changed
Whether the mutant was generated by a human or a tool
items.explanation: The kill/survive outcome is decided purely by the test suite's pass/fail result against that mutant — nothing about how the mutant was produced.

items.prompt: Which of these is an example of the "conditional boundary" mutation operator?
choices: Changing `if (age >= 18)` to `if (age > 18)`
Changing `a + b` to `a - b`
Deleting an entire if-block
Changing `return total` to `return 0`
items.explanation: Conditional boundary mutations specifically alter comparison operators at thresholds — the other options are arithmetic replacement, statement removal, and return-value mutation respectively.
items.reference:
Boundary> ↔ >=
Arithmetic+ ↔ -
Removala line deleted
Return-valuewrong constant returned

Why: each operator is a narrow, independent probe for a distinct kind of real mistake — a suite can be strong on one and blind on another.

items.prompt: What specific question does a conditional-boundary mutant test?
choices: Whether any test uses the exact boundary value of that comparison, not just values comfortably on either side
Whether the function under test has any tests at all
Whether the code compiles without warnings
Whether the function's name accurately describes what it does
items.explanation: A test comfortably past or below a threshold gives the same branch outcome regardless of `>` vs `>=` — only a test at the exact boundary value can kill this kind of mutant.
items.reference:
Boundary> ↔ >=
Arithmetic+ ↔ -
Removala line deleted
Return-valuewrong constant returned

Why: each operator is a narrow, independent probe for a distinct kind of real mistake — a suite can be strong on one and blind on another.

items.prompt: Which of these is an example of "arithmetic operator replacement"?
choices: Changing `total * 0.9` to `total / 0.9`
Changing `if (x > 5)` to `if (x >= 5)`
Deleting a variable declaration entirely
Renaming a function without changing its logic
items.explanation: Arithmetic operator replacement swaps one arithmetic operator for another (`*` for `/`, `+` for `-`) — the other options are conditional boundary, statement removal, and an unrelated rename.

items.prompt: What kind of real programmer mistake does arithmetic operator replacement model?
choices: A sign or operator typo, like writing `-` where `+` was meant
A missing semicolon at the end of a statement
A misspelled variable name
An unused import left in the file
items.explanation: It's modeled on the common, easy-to-make mistake of using the wrong arithmetic operator — a plausible typo, not a random corruption.

items.prompt: What does the "statement removal" mutation operator do?
choices: Deletes a line of code entirely, to check whether any test would notice it's missing
Renames a variable consistently throughout the file
Adds an extra, unrelated line of code
Changes the file's indentation only
items.explanation: Statement removal mutants delete a line outright — a real analogue of a forgotten line, or dead code accidentally cut during a merge.

items.prompt: A statement-removal mutant deletes a surcharge line inside an `if` block, and the mutant survives. What does that tell you?
choices: No test enters that branch with a value where the surcharge's presence or absence is actually observable in the assertion
The `if` block itself has a syntax error
The surcharge line was already dead code with no effect
Coverage for that branch must be 0%
items.explanation: The branch may well be covered — the gap is that no test's expected value depends on whether that specific line ran, so removing it goes unnoticed.

items.prompt: A module generates 50 mutants; 35 are killed, 15 survive, and none are equivalent. What's the mutation score?
items.explanation: 35 killed ÷ 50 total non-equivalent mutants = 70%.

items.prompt: A module generates 20 mutants; 18 are killed, 2 survive but both are confirmed equivalent mutants. What's the mutation score?
items.explanation: The 2 equivalent mutants are excluded from the denominator: 18 killed ÷ 18 non-equivalent mutants = 100%.

items.prompt: A module generates 10 mutants; 4 are killed, 6 survive, and 1 of the survivors is confirmed equivalent. What's the mutation score (rounded)?
items.explanation: One survivor is equivalent, so the denominator is 10 − 1 = 9 non-equivalent mutants: 4 killed ÷ 9 ≈ 44%.

items.prompt: Why don't most teams run mutation testing on every single commit?
choices: Cost multiplies — generating N mutants means rerunning the entire suite N times, far slower than running it once
Mutation testing tools don't exist for most programming languages
It would always give the exact same result as coverage, making it redundant
It requires rewriting every existing test from scratch first
items.explanation: The combinatorial cost (mutants × suite runtime) makes it too slow for the inner dev loop — the same suite gets rerun once per mutant.

items.prompt: Per L2, how do teams typically scope mutation testing in practice?
choices: To critical modules (e.g. pricing, auth), run periodically like a nightly CI job, rather than gating every pull request
Across the entire codebase, on every single commit, as a hard merge gate
Only ever run once, at project kickoff
Only on files that currently have 0% line coverage
items.explanation: Given the combinatorial cost, teams scope it to the highest-stakes modules and run it on a periodic cadence, treating the result as a diagnostic signal rather than a merge gate.

items.prompt: correctSurcharge and mutantSurcharge differ only by a conditional-boundary mutation (`>` became `>=`). Complete killsMutant(weightKg) so it returns true exactly when calling both functions with that weightKg would produce different results — i.e. that input would kill the mutant.

tests.description: the exact boundary value (20) kills the mutant
a value comfortably past the boundary does not kill the mutant
a value comfortably below the boundary does not kill the mutant

items.explanation: Only the exact boundary value (20) makes the two comparisons disagree — `20 > 20` is false but `20 >= 20` is true. Any value comfortably above or below the threshold gives the same branch outcome under both operators, so it can never kill a conditional-boundary mutant.
items.reference:
🎯 only the exact boundary value can distinguish > from >= (whichever direction the mutation flipped)
❌ values comfortably on either side give the same branch outcome under both

Why: a conditional-boundary mutant tests whether the suite has a test sitting exactly on the threshold — nothing less specific can kill it.

items.prompt: correctDiscount and mutantDiscount differ only by a conditional-boundary mutation (`>=` became `>`). Complete killsMutant(distanceKm) so it returns true exactly when calling both functions with that distanceKm would produce different results.

tests.description: the exact boundary value (500) kills the mutant
a value comfortably past the boundary does not kill the mutant
a value comfortably below the boundary does not kill the mutant

items.explanation: At exactly 500, the original `>=` applies the discount while the mutant's `>` withholds it — they disagree only at that exact value. Anywhere else, both comparisons agree on which branch to take.
items.reference:

tests.description: the exact boundary value (65) kills the mutant
a value comfortably past the boundary does not kill the mutant
a value comfortably below the boundary does not kill the mutant

items.explanation: At exactly 65, `>=` counts the person eligible while `>` doesn't — the only input where the two comparisons disagree. Every other age gives the same eligibility result under both.

items.prompt: correctFee and mutantFee differ only by an arithmetic-operator-replacement mutation (`*` became `/`). Complete killsMutant(weightKg) so it returns true exactly when the two functions disagree for that weightKg.

tests.description: a typical positive weight kills the mutant
zero does not kill the mutant (0 * 0.5 equals 0 / 0.5)
another typical positive weight kills the mutant

items.explanation: Multiplying and dividing by 0.5 only agree when the input is 0 — every nonzero weight produces a different result under `*` versus `/`, so almost any realistic test value kills this mutant, unlike a conditional-boundary mutant which needs the exact threshold.
items.reference:
✳️ a swapped arithmetic operator (*//, +/-) usually diverges from the original for almost any nonzero input, agreeing only at a degenerate value like 0
✅ almost any nonzero test value kills this kind of mutant

Why: arithmetic-operator mutants are usually easy to kill — unlike boundary mutants, they don't need a precise, hard-to-guess input value.

items.prompt: correctFee and mutantFee differ only by an arithmetic-operator-replacement mutation (`+` became `-`). Complete killsMutant(base, surcharge) so it returns true exactly when the two functions disagree for those inputs.

tests.description: a nonzero surcharge kills the mutant
a zero surcharge does not kill the mutant (base + 0 equals base - 0)
another nonzero surcharge kills the mutant

items.explanation: `base + surcharge` and `base - surcharge` only agree when surcharge is 0 — any nonzero surcharge kills this mutant, since addition and subtraction diverge immediately once there's something nonzero to add or subtract.
items.reference:
✳️ a swapped arithmetic operator (*//, +/-) usually diverges from the original for almost any nonzero input, agreeing only at a degenerate value like 0
✅ almost any nonzero test value kills this kind of mutant

Why: arithmetic-operator mutants are usually easy to kill — unlike boundary mutants, they don't need a precise, hard-to-guess input value.

items.prompt: correctFee and mutantFee differ only in that the mutant has the heavy-package surcharge line deleted. Complete killsMutant(weightKg) so it returns true exactly when the two functions disagree for that weightKg.

tests.description: a weight past the surcharge threshold kills the mutant
a weight below the threshold does not kill the mutant (the deleted line never ran either way)
another weight past the threshold kills the mutant

items.explanation: The deleted line only matters once the `if` branch is entered — a weight under 20 never reaches that line in either version, so it can't reveal the deletion. Only a weight that actually enters the surcharge branch exposes the missing statement.
items.reference:
🗑️ a deleted line only matters if a test actually reaches it
✅ reaching the branch and checking the resulting value both matter

Why: statement-removal mutants test whether any test's expected value would actually change if that exact line vanished.

items.prompt: correctFee and mutantFee differ only in that the mutant has the long-distance discount line deleted. Complete killsMutant(distanceKm) so it returns true exactly when the two functions disagree for that distanceKm.

tests.description: a distance past the discount threshold kills the mutant
a distance below the threshold does not kill the mutant
the exact threshold distance kills the mutant

items.explanation: The deleted discount line only matters once the `if` branch is entered — a distance under 500 never reaches it in either version. Any distance that enters the branch (including exactly 500) exposes the missing statement.

items.prompt: correctIsEligible and mutantIsEligible differ only by a return-value mutation (the mutant always returns true). Complete killsMutant(score) so it returns true exactly when the two functions disagree for that score.

tests.description: a failing score kills the mutant (correct says false, mutant says true)
a passing score does not kill the mutant (both agree it's true)
another failing score kills the mutant

items.explanation: Since the mutant always returns true, it only disagrees with the correct function when the correct answer is false — i.e. any score below the threshold. A suite that only ever tests passing scores would let this mutant survive completely.
items.reference:
🔁 a return-value mutant ignores the input and always returns one fixed value
🎯 only a test expecting the other outcome can kill it

Why: if a suite only ever tests inputs on one side of a decision, a mutant that hardcodes that one outcome sails through undetected.

a spend below the threshold does not kill the mutant (both agree it's false)
the exact boundary spend does not kill the mutant (correct is false there too)

items.explanation: Since the mutant always returns false, it only disagrees with the correct function when the correct answer is true — i.e. any spend strictly above 1000. A suite that never tests a genuinely premium-tier spend would let this mutant survive completely.

Why: if a suite only ever tests inputs on one side of a decision, a mutant that hardcodes that one outcome sails through undetected.

items.prompt: A mutation-testing tool flags a mutant that reorders `a + b + c` to `b + a + c` as "survived," and no possible test can kill it. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: It's an equivalent mutant — the change never affects observable behavior, so no test could ever kill it
It's a real gap that needs a new test written immediately
The mutation-testing tool itself is broken
Coverage for that line must be 0%
items.explanation: Addition is commutative, so reordering the operands produces identical output for every input — this is a false survivor, not a real test gap. No test can distinguish behavior that never actually changed.
items.reference:
🧬 mutant changes the code but not its observable behavior
🚫 no test, no matter how thorough, can ever kill it

Why: a survivor is only a real gap if some possible test could have killed it — equivalent mutants fail that condition by definition.

items.prompt: Why can't a mutation-testing tool automatically tell you whether a survivor is a real gap or an equivalent mutant?
choices: Deciding whether two programs behave identically for every possible input is undecidable in general, so a human has to review survivors
Because the tool doesn't have access to any test data at that point
Because equivalent mutants are actually impossible for any tool to generate
Because it's a licensing restriction in most mutation-testing tools
items.explanation: General program equivalence is undecidable — no algorithm can determine for arbitrary code whether two versions always behave the same. Tools flag survivors; a human still has to judge which ones are equivalent.
items.reference:
🧬 mutant changes the code but not its observable behavior
🚫 no test, no matter how thorough, can ever kill it

Why: a survivor is only a real gap if some possible test could have killed it — equivalent mutants fail that condition by definition.

items.prompt: Per L3's cost table, why does mutation testing get expensive fast as mutant count grows?
choices: The full test suite reruns once per mutant, so total time scales with mutants × suite runtime
Each mutant requires manually writing a brand-new test suite from scratch
Mutants are generated one at a time by a human reviewer
The cost is fixed regardless of how many mutants are generated
items.explanation: Total runtime is mutants × suite runtime — doubling either one roughly doubles total time, which is why even a modest mutant count on a modest suite adds up fast.

items.prompt: Why do teams typically scope mutation testing to critical modules (pricing, auth) instead of the whole codebase?
choices: Given the combinatorial cost, it's more valuable to spend that cost where a missed logic bug is expensive, rather than spreading it evenly
Mutation testing tools technically only work on pricing and auth code
Other modules never contain any bugs worth catching
It's a legal requirement for financial and authentication code specifically
items.explanation: Since the technique is expensive to run broadly, teams prioritize it where a silent logic bug is costliest — high-stakes modules — rather than running it uniformly everywhere.

items.prompt: Per L3, what's the typical cadence for running mutation testing, and how should a survivor list be treated?
choices: Run periodically (e.g. a nightly or weekly CI job); treat survivors as a diagnostic signal to act on, not a merge-blocking gate
Run on every single pull request and block the merge until the mutation score reaches 100%
Run exactly once, at project kickoff, and never again
Run only manually, whenever a production incident occurs
items.explanation: Given the cost, mutation testing runs on a periodic cadence rather than gating every commit, and its output is meant to guide where to add tests — not to block merges the way a linter or the test suite itself does.
